section_summary: This section consists of State Department docket list pages (1930–1934) followed by five complete monthly political reports and the start of a sixth from the American Embassy in Tokyo covering July through December 1931. The reports document the rapid escalation of the Manchurian crisis from the Wanpaoshan affair and the murder of Captain Nakamura to the Mukden Incident of September 18 and subsequent Japanese military campaigns toward Tsitsihar and Chinchow. They also detail severe domestic political and economic developments, including the death of former Premier Hamaguchi, the resignation of Dr. Egi, the collapse of the Wakatsuki Cabinet over coalition negotiations, widespread labor distress, banking pressures leading to the abandonment of the gold standard, and notable visits by foreign aviators including Charles Lindbergh.

subfiles.about: State Department docket list indexing monthly political reports on conditions in Japan from February 1930 to July 1934.
subfiles.summary: Docket indexes monthly political-report despatches on Japan, February 1930-July 1934, listing serial numbers, dates, officers (Castle, Neville, Forbes, Grew), and decimal cross-references across years of regional turbulence.
subfiles.title: List of Papers: Political Reports on Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 58 on political and economic conditions in Japan during July 1931.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 291 transmits the Embassy's monthly political review for July 1931, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams sent. The report highlights severe anti-Chinese riots in Korea and Manchuria sparked by the Wanpaoshan dispute, resulting in major casualties in Heijo and heavy criticism of the Government-General. It also covers the public trial of forty Japanese Communist Party leaders, the merger of proletarian parties into the Zenkoku Ronotaishuto, rising unemployment aggravated by naval retrenchment under the London Naval Treaty, and the discreet visit of Canton Foreign Minister Eugene Chen.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 291: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for July 1931 (Report No. 58)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 59 on political, military, and economic conditions in Japan during August 1931.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 324 transmits the monthly report for August 1931, detailing extensive aviation activities including the enthusiastic reception given to Colonel and Mrs. Charles Lindbergh, contrasted with the bureaucratic arrest and fining of aviators Hugh Herndon, Jr. and Clyde Pangborn. It analyzes the controversial speech by Minister of War Minami criticizing disarmament and emphasizing Manchurian-Mongolian defense, fierce cabinet budget battles, and the inflammatory murder of Staff Officer Captain Nakamura by Chinese troops. Other sections note the departure of Eugene Chen, the death of former Premier Hamaguchi from his assassination wounds, and a violent strike at General Motors Japan.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 324: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for August 1931 (Report No. 59)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 60 on Japanese internal and foreign affairs during September 1931.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 351 forwards the monthly report for September 1931, which chronicles the outbreak of the Manchurian Incident on September 18 following the explosion on the South Manchuria Railway at Peitaying, leading to the rapid seizure of Mukden, Changchun, and Kirin by Japanese troops. It reviews the commemoration of the 1923 earthquake and a severe new shock on September 21, the resolution of Herndon and Pangborn's legal troubles, and administrative reorganizations marked by Dr. Egi's resignation as Minister of Railways. Additional topics include ongoing northern fishery disputes with Soviet authorities, the temporary closing of the Tokyo Stock Exchange after Britain abandoned the gold standard, and Japan's submission of armaments figures to the League of Nations.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 351: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for September 1931 (Report No. 60)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 61 on Japanese political, financial, and foreign developments during October 1931.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 379 submits Report No. 61, documenting the consolidation of Japanese military positions across Manchuria, the aerial bombing of Chinchow, and the civilian cabinet's inability to restrain the military element. It evaluates the Minseito's substantial victory in prefectural elections, the murder trial of Hamaguchi's assailant Tomeo Sagoya, and the military's successful insistence on the Emperor attending autumn manoeuvres in Kyushu instead of remaining in Tokyo for the League of Nations session. In finance, it highlights two discount rate hikes by the Bank of Japan to stem gold outflow, the severe depression in the shipping trade due to Chinese boycotts and British sterling depreciation, Herndon and Pangborn's non-stop transpacific flight, and the death of Dr. Mitsugu Sengoku.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 379: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for October 1931 (Report No. 61)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 62 covering political, military, and financial events in Japan during November 1931.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy (for the Ambassador), Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 404 transmits the November 1931 report, detailing major military clashes in northern Manchuria at the Nonni River bridge, the routing of General Ma Zhanshan's forces, the occupation of Tsitsihar, and an aborted Japanese advance toward Chinchow that was halted by orders from Tokyo. It examines domestic political turmoil triggered by Home Minister Adachi's unilateral public call for a coalition cabinet, causing a major cabinet crisis. The report also describes severe financial strains resulting in massive gold specie exports to the United States, intensifying domestic agitation for an embargo on gold exports, a sharply reduced rice harvest, the collapse of export trade with China, and the death of Viscount Eiichi Shibusawa.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 404: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for November 1931 (Report No. 62)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 63 covering Japanese diplomatic and military developments during December 1931 (incomplete).
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 458 and the initial portion of Report No. 63 discuss relations with the United States regarding Secretary of State Stimson's press remarks and his December 22 memorandum concerning Chinchow. The report explains that Japanese press and public opinion considered foreign representations regarding Chinchow unwarranted, viewing the military advance against Marshal Chang Hsueh-liang's forces as justified under the League of Nations' December 10 resolution. The document section breaks off mid-sentence at the beginning of the section reviewing relations with Soviet Russia.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 458: Transmitting Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for December 1931 (Report No. 63)
